reports.title: Average weekly earnings
reports.description: The lead monthly measure of average weekly earnings per employee in Great Britain, published as the 'Average weekly earnings in Great Britain' bulletin and as the EARN datasets. AWE is the ratio of estimated total pay for the whole economy to the total number of employees, calculated from the Monthly Wages and Salaries Survey, whose sample is drawn from the Inter-Departmental Business Register; pay for employees of businesses below the MWSS size threshold is estimated from the Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings. Published for total pay and regular pay, and in real terms deflated by consumer price inflation. Excludes the self-employed, HM armed forces and government-supported trainees.

reports.title: Workforce jobs
reports.description: The quarterly measure of the number of jobs in the UK and ONS's preferred measure of short-term employment change by industry, published as the workforce jobs element of the 'Vacancies and jobs in the UK' bulletin and as the JOBS datasets. WFJ is the sum of employee jobs, self-employment jobs, government-supported trainees and HM forces. Employee jobs come from the Quarterly Business Survey and the Quarterly Public Sector Employment Survey and are benchmarked annually to the Business Register and Employment Survey; self-employment jobs and the England government-supported-trainee component come from the Labour Force Survey; the public-sector boundary is the one defined by the UK National Accounts.

This is the reverse of gb-ons-workforce-jobs -> gb-ons-national-accounts and the round had held it in _dropped as `deferred`, because minting both makes the pair MUTUAL and a mutual pair is excluded from `rankedEdges` (it is a 2-cycle that pumps its own authority). Thomas ruled to mint anyway: both directions are real and different — WFJ takes its public-sector boundary from the National Accounts, and the National Accounts consume WFJ employment data — and the corpus should say so even at the cost of the pair's PageRank contribution. The quoted span is the list item that names this target. GRADED B, not A: a source-disclosure list is thinner than a figure source line, and Thomas's caption ruling was about captions, not bullets — under-claimed deliberately. Note for a future round: the same list would support edges to Productivity and to Household Income, neither of which is a node. REFUSED 2026-09-06 (round 4). The AWE QMI's concepts section says 'This classification follows the UK National Accounts Sector Classifications conventions', describing how the MWSS sample is stratified by public or private legal status. That names the sector classification conventions, which ONS publishes as the Public sector classification guide, not the UK National Accounts / Blue Book that gb-ons-national-accounts stands for. Under the 2026-09-05 organisation-versus-instrument ruling the named artefact is the classification guide, which has no node. Recorded so the sentence is not re-derived as a Blue Book edge.

DOCUMENTED NEGATIVE 2026-09-06 (round 4), and worth having as one. The AWE QMI's concepts and definitions section says in consecutive sentences: 'The main source for average weekly earnings (AWE), the Monthly Wages and Salaries Survey, is a statutory survey carried out in accordance with the 1947 Statistics of Trade Act. The production of AWE is not specifically required by any legislation, but is driven primarily by the requirements of HM Treasury and the Bank of England.' The Statistics of Trade Act 1947 is the legal basis of the SURVEY, not of the statistic, and ONS says explicitly that no legislation requires AWE. So no legal_basis edge from gb-ons-awe, and the Act (no node) would be the wrong target for one anyway. The GB legislation family gained five instruments this week; this records why AWE is not a sixth customer.
